the external requirement. When PH01 is absent from your allowed manifest,
mark the internal basis N/A.

units assigned to LC in the current card. Lock your response before you
receive colleagues' answers. For each reporting or notification path give
its own trigger, awareness point, clock, recipient, channel, and next step.

• Q03 · COM. a. Decide how and when to alert affected or likely affected customers about the service disruption. b. Decide whether to publish a public holding statement, through which channel and with what approval.

[R05] HKMA circular Incident response and management procedures (2010-06-22, scanned original)

[This PDF is a scan with no text layer. The text below is an OCR transcription made for searching; paragraph wrapping is normalised. The PDF is the authoritative copy: check any quotation against the PDF.]

=== PDF page 1 ===
Hong Kong Monetary Authority
香港金融管理局

Our Ref: B1/15C, B9/29C
Arthur K. H. Yuen JP, Deputy Chief Executive
阮國恒 JP，副總裁

22 June 2010

The Chief Executive

All Authorized Institutions

Dear Sir/Madam,

Incident response and management procedures

In the light of several significant incidents that have affected a number of authorized institutions (AIs) recently, I am writing to remind AIs of the need to have effective incident response and management capability and procedures to deal with significant incidents and to set out the relevant principles that AIs should follow in any public communication in respect of such incidents.

It is recognised that every incident is different and how best to deal with a particular case will depend on the circumstances of the case. It is nevertheless important for all AIs to ensure that whenever any significant incident occurs, they take the actions set out below:

Immediate incident response

The AI concerned should immediately analyse the cause of the incident and as soon as practicable rectify or contain the problem. The top priority should be to safeguard the interests of customers who have been or may be affected by the incident.

Customer notifications

The AI concerned should also determine as quickly as possible after identifying an incident whether the situation is likely to affect other customers or the customers of other AIs (for example where the incident relates to the use of shared Automatic Teller Machine (ATM) networks).

The AI should proactively notify the customers affected or likely to be affected through the most effective means and advise them of the steps or precautionary measures that they need to take as well as whether the bank would reimburse any losses incurred by them and if so, how they can apply for compensation e.g. by calling enquiry hotlines. Where necessary, the AI

=== PDF page 2 ===
should also notify other affected AIs (so that they can in turn notify their affected customers) as soon as practicable.

Public announcement

In addition to notifying the customers individually, it is also important for the AI concerned to consider making a public announcement where the situation so warrants, such as in the following circumstances:

(a) where the nature of the incident is serious, for example if the incident entails the disruption of any essential and critical banking service channel (e.g. branch services, e-banking, ATM services, etc.) or the disruption may last for a prolonged period of time; or

(b) where a large number of customers have been or may be affected, especially when public announcement is one of the faster or more effective means to alert such customers of the incident than individual notifications.

In notifying the customers and making a public announcement, the AI concerned should include the key facts of the incident and the steps that affected customers need to take in the circumstances in order to gain or regain access to the relevant banking services or to protect their interests.

The above are only the broad principles that an AI should consider and there could be other relevant factors that the AI should also take into account. For example, the need to keep the public informed may need to be weighed against the relevant legal considerations, including where appropriate whether a public announcement may prejudice any ongoing criminal proceedings or any investigation. The important point is that the actions taken to keep the customers and, where appropriate, the public informed of a significant incident should form an integral part of the incident response and management capability of AIs. If in doubt, AIs should consult the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

Reporting incident to the HKMA

In addition, once an AI has become aware that a significant incident has occurred, the AI concerned should notify the HKMA immediately and provide it with whatever information is available at the time. For the avoidance of doubt, an AI should not wait until it has rectified the problem before reporting the incident to the HKMA. The HKMA may require the AI concerned to provide further information or updates. Depending on the nature and seriousness of the incident and on whether the incident has wider implications for the general public, the HKMA may make a separate public announcement as appropriate.

=== PDF page 3 ===
Handling of customers’ and media’s enquiry

When handling a significant incident affecting a substantial number of customers, the AI concerned is likely to receive a large number of customer and media enquiries. It is therefore essential for the AI concerned to deploy swiftly adequate resources and communication channels (e.g. customer service hotlines and extended office hours of branch services) to handle such enquiries. In addition, a proper communication strategy should be formulated by the senior management to ensure that consistent and up-to-date messages are conveyed to all relevant parties on a timely basis. The HKMA should be kept informed during the process and copies of public communication materials should be submitted to the HKMA for reference.

AIs should ensure that their staff members are at all times alert to the importance of detecting significant incidents and reporting such incidents to senior management. AIs are expected to ensure that they have in place the appropriate incident response and management capability. The HKMA will continue to assess the adequacy and effectiveness of AIs’ incident response and management capability and procedures through its ongoing supervisory efforts.

Should you have any questions on the content of this letter, please feel free to contact Mr Nelson Chow at 2878 1470 or Mr George Chou at 2878 1599.

7.3 Obligation to notify computer-system security incidents
7.3.1 The purpose of a CI operator notifying the Commissioner of a computer-system
security incident is to enable the Commissioner to assess the overall consequences for
the continuous provision of essential services in one or multiple sectors, or for the
maintenance of critical societal or economic activities in Hong Kong, and to take
appropriate remedial measures to prevent the impact from spreading to other sectors.
7.3.2 A computer-system security incident must involve access or any other act performed
without lawful authority and that has an actual adverse effect to the CCSs involved.
An event arising from pure technical failure, natural disaster, mass power outage, a
computer-system security threat that is detected and timely removed or quarantined,
or personal data leakage arising from human mistake, does not constitute a computer-
system security incident.
7.3.3 Examples of computer-system security incidents include but are not limited to:
(a) Large-scale or volumetric Distributed DoS (“DDoS”) attack causing
degradation of an essential service, or Ransom DDoS attack where a ransom
note is received;
(b) Ransomware attack that causes suspension of an essential service or shows
signs of data compromise;
(c) Unintended external connection to a CCS caused by malware infection or by
an adversary exploiting a vulnerability;
(d) An employee accesses to sensitive digital data of a CCS and maliciously
exfiltrates that data or maliciously misconfigures the access privilege of the
CCS;
(e) Configurations or data of a CCS are modified by a malicious payload or script;
(f) An employee abuses his / her authority to interfere with the functioning of the
CCS; and
(g) Any tampering with cryptographic key management devices that hampers the
normal functioning of a CCS.
7.3.4 A serious computer-system security incident is an incident which has disrupted, is
disrupting or is likely to disrupt the core function of the CI concerned, and must be
notified within 12 hours after the CI operator becomes aware of it. An incident is
considered as a serious incident if any of the below criteria are met:
(a) The downtime affecting the core function of the CI concerned has exceeded or
is likely to exceed the maximum tolerable downtime defined by the CI operator
in the business continuity management plan;
(b) The service performance has dropped or is likely to drop below the minimum
service level defined by the CI operator in the business continuity management
plan;

=== PDF page 36 ===
Page 36 of 51
(c) The computer-system security incident has triggered or is likely to trigger the
activation of business continuity or disaster recovery procedures;
(d) The computer-system security incident has caused or is likely to cause the
leakage of material volume of customer data, where “material” is defined by
the CI operator in the business continuity management plan;
(e) The computer-system security incident has leaked or is likely to leak sensitive
digital data that hampers the normal functioning of the CCS;
(f) The computer-system security incident has caused or is likely to cause a
material number of customer enquiries or complaints, where “material” is
defined by the CI operator in the business continuity management plan; or
(g) Threat actors have threatened to launch an attack against a CCS at a specified
time that would likely trigger any of the scenario described in sections 7.3.4(a)
to (f).
7.3.5 When the CI operator discovers any sign of disruption or irregularity in the CCSs, the
CI operator may need to spend time to ascertain whether a computer-system security
incident has occurred. At the point the CI operator has a reasonable degree of certainty
that a computer-system security incident has occurred, the CI operator is deemed to
have become aware of the computer-system security incident.
7.3.6 Notification in Specified Form
(a) When a CI operator becomes aware that a computer-system security incident
has occurred, the CI operator should notify the Commissioner by submitting a
specified form (Annex E or a sector-specific form) through a designated
secured channel. The CI operator should complete the form as far as
practicable based on the information available.
(b) Alternatively, the CI operator may first make the notification to a designated
telephone number, providing the below information, and then submit a
specified form (Annex E or a sector-specific form) through a designated
secured channel within 48 hours of the notification:
(i) Nature of the computer-system security incident;
(ii) CCSs involved; and
(iii) Brief incident summary.
(c) For the avoidance of doubt, the CI operator is obliged to fulfil any sector
specific requirements in incident notification imposed by the relevant
regulatory regime or other applicable laws.

1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Purpose and scope
1.1.1 This Sectoral Code of Practice (this Code) is published by the Monetary Authority
(the MA) in consultation with the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-
system Security) (the Commissioner) pursuant to section 8 of the Protection of Critical
Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (the Ordinance).
1.1.2 This Code is applicable to an Authorized Institution (AI) designated by the MA as a
Critical Infrastructure (CI) operator (Designated AI).
1.1.3 This Code provides practical guidance on how a Designated AI complies with
category 1 obligations and category 2 obligations. A Designated AI should refer to
guidance published by the Commissioner in relation to category 3 obligations, which
can be found in section 7 of the Code of Practice (Generic) published on the website
of the Office of the Commissioner (hyperlink to
https://www.occics.gov.hk/en/industry/code-of-practice/index.html).
1.1.4 A Designated AI should refer to relevant sections and/or schedules of the Ordinance
at all times when applying guidance provided in this Code to ensure compliance with
legal obligations.
1.1.5 This Code is not subsidiary legislation, nor would failure to comply with the
provisions of this Code in itself constitute an offence. However, the MA may issue
written directions to require a Designated AI to take appropriate actions in relation to
the compliance with category 1 obligations and category 2 obligations if there has
been non-compliance or defective compliance with such obligations, which may be
considered with reference to this Code. Failure to comply with such directions would
be an offence.
1.1.6 A Designated AI should provide information, which is accessible in or from Hong
Kong, to the MA upon request in relation to the compliance with category 1
obligations and category 2 obligations.
1.1.7 This Code sets the baseline requirements for protecting critical computer systems
(CCSs) of Designated AIs, and does not target personal data nor trade secrets of
Designated AIs. A Designated AI should apply enhanced security measures,
appropriate to its circumstances and commensurate with the computer-system security
risk of its CCSs.
1.1.8 The MA may, in consultation with the Commissioner and industry stakeholders, from
time to time review and amend the requirements stipulated in this Code according to
the latest technological development and industry best practices.

# Lan Tidal Bank Limited — Cyber Incident Response Playbook (PH01)

Internal bank procedure. Version 1.0, approved by the Chief Executive on behalf of the Board Risk Committee, effective 1 October 2026. Owner: Head of Information Security. Next review: 30 September 2027.

Lan Tidal Bank Limited is a fictional bank. This playbook is exercise material.


## 1. Purpose, status and use

1.1 This playbook sets the bank's own operating procedure for a cyber incident that disrupts a critical operation or exposes customer data. It covers who decides, in what order, through which channel, and what record is kept.

1.2 It is an internal procedure. It does not create, restate or replace any statutory, supervisory or regulatory requirement. Where it refers to an external requirement it names the document only; staff must read and apply the external document itself.

1.3 Where this playbook and an external requirement differ, the external requirement prevails. The person who notices the difference records it in the decision log and tells the Head of Legal and Compliance at once.

1.4 Internal times in this playbook are the bank's own targets. They never extend an external deadline.

=== PDF page 2 ===
## 2. Incident command

2.1 **Crisis Management Team (CMT).** Chair: Chief Executive; alternate: Chief Operating Officer. Members: Head of Information Security (SEC), Head of Legal and Compliance (LC), Head of Corporate Communications (COM), Head of Payments Operations, Head of IT Operations, Chief Risk Officer, Data Protection Officer. The chair convenes the CMT within 30 minutes of a severity 1 or 2 declaration (section 4).

2.2 **Decision log.** The CMT keeps one master decision log from the first minute. Every decision is entered with: decision, owner, time (HKT), condition if any, recipient and channel, and status (executed, scheduled, held, not executed). Other registers (evidence, regulator contacts, customer notifications, cases) are cross-referenced to it.

2.3 **Preconditions.** Before an action is made to wait on a condition, the condition is logged with four items: who verifies it; the latest time by which it must be verified; the default action if it is not verified by then; and a close-out entry when it is verified or the default is applied. A condition without these four items is not valid and does not hold the action. The default action may be to go ahead, to hold, or to switch to an alternate process approved under section 8. Reconciliation, security and applicable compliance conditions, including every item of the gate in 9.3, stay in force when their time passes: for these the default is to hold or to switch to an approved alternate process, never to go ahead. Where the default is to go ahead, the missing confirmation or evidence is obtained and logged afterwards. Reports to regulators and authorities are never held by an internal condition; they follow 2.4.

2.4 **External reports are not held by internal confirmation.** Internal review of a report to a regulator or authority runs in parallel with the report, not before it. The initial report goes on the facts held at the time, with unverified items marked as unverified; the results of internal checks go in the next update. No internal condition, review or approval may delay an action needed to meet an external deadline. If an internal condition is still open 30 minutes before the external deadline, the default in 2.3 applies and the report goes by a route that meets the requirement for that report (5.6).

2.5 **Status reports.** SEC reports to the chair every hour until containment is confirmed, then every four hours. Each report states what has changed, what is confirmed, what is unverified and what is due next.

## 4. Severity, tolerance and BCP activation

4.1 **Severity 1:** a critical operation is disrupted, or customer personal data is confirmed or suspected to be exposed, or an extortion demand is received. **Severity 2:** a critical operation is degraded but working, or a security event affects a critical system without confirmed disruption. **Severity 3:** other security events.

4.2 **Critical operations and tolerance for disruption (Board-approved).**

| Critical operation | Maximum tolerable disruption |
|---|---|
| Outbound domestic transfers and SME payroll submission | 24 hours |
| Customer access to balances (mobile and branches) | 8 hours |
| Card authorisation | 4 hours |

4.3 When a disruption reaches 50% of its tolerance, the CMT chair tells the Board chair. When it reaches 100%, the CMT chair convenes the Board or its Risk Committee (section 15).

4.4 **BCP activation is declared, not assumed.** The CMT chair declares activation of the business continuity plan in the decision log, with the time and the operation concerned, whenever alternate processing, an alternate site or a manual workaround is authorised for a critical operation. LC is told at once so that any external reporting that follows from activation is made.

=== PDF page 5 ===
## 5. Regulator, authority and external reporting

5.1 **Ownership.** LC owns every report to a regulator or authority and the Regulator Contact Register (RCR). SEC supplies technical facts; COM supplies copies of public material.

5.2 **External requirements to apply.** LC applies these documents directly, as they stand on the day: the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653), section 28 and Schedule 6, and the Commissioner's Code of Practice section 7.3 and its Annexes E and F; the HKMA circular "Incident response and management procedures" (22 June 2010); SPM TM-E-1 section 8.2; SPM TM-G-2 section 1.3; the HKMA circular "Customer Data Protection" (14 October 2014); the PCPD Guidance on Data Breach Handling and the Data Breach Notification Form. This playbook does not restate their triggers, recipients or time limits.

5.3 **Deadline tracker.** At declaration LC opens a deadline tracker. Each external clock is computed from its own starting point as stated in the external document, entered with its source reference, and checked by a second LC officer within 30 minutes.

5.4 **Contacts and channels.** The RCR holds the current names, numbers, out-of-hours routes and filing addresses for the HKMA supervisory team, the Commissioner's office, the PCPD and the Police Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau. It is printed and kept in the CMT room and in the LC duty pack, so it is available if corporate systems are down.

5.5 **Evidence of every contact.** For every call, filing or letter LC records: time, channel, the name and post of the person reached, any reference number, a summary of what was said or sent, and the receipt. For an electronic filing, LC saves the system's submission receipt or dispatch record at the moment of filing. If no receipt is shown, LC asks the recipient for one in the same call or by return, and logs the request.

5.6 **Submission route and standby device.** For each written report, LC first confirms from the external document the form and the way of submission that report requires, and records them in the deadline tracker. Compliance keeps a standby filing device that is not connected to production systems. At declaration Compliance tests the standby device and logs whether it works and is enrolled for each designated channel likely to be needed; if it is not, Compliance arranges another permitted route at once and logs it. If the normal filing terminal is unavailable or under evidence hold, SEC logs within 30 minutes whether it can be released. If no decision is logged by then, LC submits from the standby device, but only if the device has been logged as working and the route meets the requirement for that report. Otherwise LC uses another route that meets the requirement, or asks the recipient which alternative it accepts and logs the answer. The receipt is saved under 5.5.

5.7 **Email.** SEC logs within 30 minutes of declaration whether corporate email is safe to use. Until it is logged as safe, written material goes by a route that does not depend on corporate email and meets the requirement for that report (5.6). An open email check never delays a report.

5.8 **Updates to the HKMA.** After the first report, LC updates the HKMA supervisory contact every four hours during the first 24 hours, then at 08:00 and 18:00 daily until the HKMA agrees otherwise, and at once on any of: BCP activation, confirmed data exposure, an extortion demand, a change in service status, a public statement.

5.9 **Later evidence.** Facts found after a report are sent as supplementary information by the route the external document sets. LC keeps one list of what each authority has been told and when.

=== PDF page 6 ===
## 6. Evidence, forensics and timeline

6.1 **Evidence hold.** At declaration SEC places an evidence hold on affected systems. No reboot, rebuild, restore, failover or deletion on a held system without SEC's logged release for that item.

6.2 **Containment comes first.** Collection of volatile evidence before containment is capped at 10 minutes. If destructive activity is still spreading, containment goes first and evidence is taken from the isolated system afterwards.

6.3 **Custody.** The evidence custodian is an SEC designate who does not administer the affected systems. Every item gets an evidence ID, source, time with clock offset, collector and witness, tool, SHA-256 hash, storage location and a transfer record. Analysis is on verified copies only.

6.4 **Clocks.** All bank systems synchronise to the bank's primary time source. Every timeline entry keeps the original timestamp, the measured offset, the normalised HKT time and its uncertainty. Events closer together than their combined uncertainty are recorded as "order undetermined".

6.5 **Retained forensic firm.** The bank has a master services agreement with a Hong Kong forensic firm. The agreement already contains the data terms in section 16. SEC may call the firm in without further approval at severity 1. This paragraph applies to the forensic firm only; suppliers of the affected systems are covered by 6.7.

6.6 **Attacker material.** Samples, demands and messages from an attacker are received only into the evidence process. Nobody requests further samples, visits attacker links or uploads attacker material to an outside service.

6.7 **Evidence held by suppliers.** This covers any supplier that supports, hosts or has remote access to an affected system.
(a) **Request.** Within one hour of declaration SEC drafts a written preservation and production request for each such supplier, covering session and access logs, account records, support tickets, change records and any bank data the supplier holds. LC clears the wording. The vendor relationship owner sends it to the contract contact in the third-party register kept by the Chief Risk Officer, and confirms receipt by call-back to a number already on file.
(b) **Channel.** Records come in only as native exports with a SHA-256 manifest, through a bank-hosted encrypted transfer or on bank-issued encrypted media collected by the evidence custodian. They are never received by ordinary email or through the supplier's own remote access path. The custodian enters them in the evidence register on receipt.
(c) **Escalation.** If the contract terms (log retention, audit and production rights) or the delivery status cannot be confirmed by the due time in the request, and in any case within four hours, the vendor relationship owner escalates to LC and the CMT chair. LC decides on formal contractual notice; the CMT chair decides any other step.
(d) **Reconciliation.** Supplier records are treated as the supplier's account until SEC has reconciled them with the bank's own logs.

LC response to C01 (Monday 16 Nov 2026, 08:00 HKT, H+0). It covers Q02a and Q02b only. Locked before I see colleagues' answers. Facilitator handoff to LC: none. All actions below are simulated, for the facilitator to log.

Facts I rely on, as released: at 08:00 the bank confirmed unauthorised commands that encrypted parts of the payment gateway, which is a designated critical computer system. Outbound domestic transfers and payroll submission are disrupted, and these are a core function of the designated infrastructure. Mobile balance view still works and branches are open. Unverified: whether failover works, the root cause, how far the attack has spread, and whether any data was exposed. Phone route to the Commissioner: verified. Terminal for the verified secure filing channel: unavailable. Dispatch log: empty.

---

**Q02a – Initial HKMA reporting**

- **Decision and action:** Report to the HKMA now by telephone to the bank's HKMA supervisory contact, using the printed Regulator Contact Register. Follow up with a short written initial report by a route that does not rely on the affected systems or on corporate email until SEC has logged email as safe. No internal review, approval or extra fact-finding may hold this report. Internal review runs alongside it.
- **What to send now:**
  - Bank name; LC as contact, with call-back numbers.
  - Awareness time: 08:00 HKT, 16 Nov.
  - Nature: confirmed unauthorised commands encrypted parts of the payment gateway (a ransomware-type act). Treated as a cyber attack.
  - Impact: outbound domestic transfers and payroll submission disrupted. Mobile balance view working. Branches open.
  - Customer exposure: 180,000 retail and 12,000 SME customers. The number actually affected is unverified. Payroll timing is a risk for SME customers.
  - Marked UNVERIFIED: whether failover works, root cause and spread, data exposure (none confirmed so far), and whether there is an extortion demand (none received so far).
  - Actions under way: containment and evidence preservation (SEC), CMT convened.
  - Parallel filings: the bank is notifying the Commissioner under Cap. 653 s.28 (Q02b). COM is preparing customer and public communications, and copies will be sent to the HKMA.
  - Next update time.
- **Owner:** LC, who owns all regulator reports (PH01 s.5.1). Executing party: LC duty officer. SEC supplies the technical facts.
- **Timing:**
  - Call target: by 08:30 HKT. The rule says "immediately"; the 30-minute figure is my professional judgment.
  - Written confirmation: target 10:00 HKT.
  - Updates: every 4 hours for the first 24 hours (12:00, 16:00, 20:00, 24:00, 04:00, 08:00), then 08:00 and 18:00 daily. Also update at once on any of: BCP activation, confirmed data exposure, an extortion demand, a change in service status, or a public statement.
- **Recipient and channel:** HKMA supervisory team, by phone. Then written follow-up by a route the HKMA accepts. I could not find an HKMA filing channel in the assigned sources, so I will ask the HKMA on the call which route it accepts and log the answer.
- **External basis:**
  - **R05**, HKMA circular "Incident response and management procedures", 22 Jun 2010 (supervisory circular, not statute). PDF p.2, heading "Reporting incident to the HKMA". Quote checked against the scan image: "once an AI has become aware that a significant incident has occurred, the AI concerned should notify the HKMA immediately and provide it with whatever information is available at the time." Also: "an AI should not wait until it has rectified the problem before reporting the incident to the HKMA."
    - Why it applies: losing a critical payment channel for a large customer base through a cyber attack is a "significant incident". That classification is my professional judgment, because the circular does not define the term.
  - **R09**, SPM TM-E-1, V.4, s.8.2.5, PDF p.33 (statutory guideline status not verified; HKMA Supervisory Policy Manual guidance). Quote: "should notify the HKMA promptly in accordance with the relevant arrangements set out by the HKMA from time to time." It does not specify the channel.
  - **R07**, SPM TM-G-2, V.2, s.1.3.3, PDF p.5. Its classification (p.1) is "A non-statutory guideline issued by the MA as a guidance note". Quote: "AIs should inform the HKMA promptly if their BCP is activated."
    - Status at this card: BCP activation has not been declared and failover is unverified.
    - Conditional action: as soon as the CMT chair declares BCP activation (PH01 s.4.4), LC tells the HKMA promptly and sends periodic progress reports.
- **Left to judgment:** the exact minutes behind "immediately", the HKMA channel, and how detailed the first report is.
- **Internal bank procedure (PH01 v1.0):**
  - s.5.1: "LC owns every report to a regulator or authority".
  - s.2.4: "The initial report goes on the facts held at the time, with unverified items marked as unverified".
  - s.5.8: "LC updates the HKMA supervisory contact every four hours during the first 24 hours".
  - s.5.7: "An open email check never delays a report."
  - s.1.4: internal times "never extend an external deadline."
  - No conflict with the external requirements.

---

**Q02b – Critical infrastructure incident notification under Cap. 653 s.28**

- **Decision:** Notification is triggered. This is a serious incident, so the 12-hour limit applies.
- **Action:**
  - Notify the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-system Security) now, by the verified telephone route.
  - On the call, give the information R02 7.3.6(b) requires:
    - (i) Nature: unauthorised commands encrypted gateway components (ransomware-type), disrupting a core function.
    - (ii) Critical computer system involved: the payment gateway.
    - (iii) Brief summary: discovered and confirmed 08:00 HKT; outbound domestic transfers and payroll disrupted; failover, root cause and data exposure unverified; containment under way.
  - Log the time, the person reached, any reference number and a summary (PH01 s.5.5). Ask for a reference or receipt in the same call.
  - Then file the specified form (Annex E or the sector form) through the designated secure channel within 48 hours of the call.
  - Because the normal terminal is down:
    - At declaration, Compliance tests and logs the standby filing device and whether it is enrolled for this channel.
    - SEC logs within 30 minutes whether the terminal can be released.
    - If neither works, LC asks the Commissioner's office during the call which alternative route it accepts, and logs the answer (PH01 s.5.6).
- **Owner:** LC. Executing party: LC duty officer. SEC supplies the facts.
- **Awareness point:** 08:00 HKT, 16 Nov 2026, when the bank "confirms" the unauthorised commands. That meets R02 7.3.5's test of "a reasonable degree of certainty".
- **Clocks:**
  - (1) Initial notification: as soon as practicable, and no later than **20:00 HKT on Mon 16 Nov**. Internal target: phone call by 09:00 HKT.
  - (2) Written record in specified form: within 48 hours of the phone notification. Example: a call at 09:00 Mon means a deadline of 09:00 Wed 18 Nov. The exact time is set from the logged call time. Target: Tue 17 Nov.
  - (3) Written report in specified form (Annex F or sector form): within 14 days after the awareness date, which I compute as by **Mon 30 Nov 2026**. That date count is my professional judgment and should be checked by a second LC officer under PH01 s.5.3. Internal target: 27 Nov. Supplementary information follows as facts emerge.
- **Recipient:** the Commissioner, not the HKMA.
  - Section 28 sits in Part 4, Division 3 (R01 PDF p.43). Under s.2 (PDF p.9), "category 3 obligation means an obligation imposed by Division 3 of Part 4".
  - R03 s.1.1.3 (PDF p.3) directs designated AIs to the Commissioner's guidance for category 3 obligations.
  - Tell the HKMA that the filing has been made, as part of the Q02a updates.
- **External basis:**
  - **R01**, Cap. 653 Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (statute; verified copy, version date 10 Sep 2026).
    - s.2 definition, PDF p.10: an event involving "access, without lawful authority" or another unlawful act that "has an actual adverse effect on the computer-system security of the critical computer system". Applied: unauthorised encryption of a designated system meets both limbs.
    - s.28(1), PDF pp.43-44: "If a CI operator becomes aware that a computer-system security incident has occurred in respect of a critical computer system ... the operator must notify the Commissioner".
    - s.28(2), PDF p.44: "as soon as practicable and in any event within the specified time". Under s.28(2)(b)(ii), a notification not made in the specified form must still "include information on the nature of the computer-system security incident and identify the critical computer system concerned".
    - s.28(3): a later written record in specified form. s.28(4): a written report.
    - s.28(5)-(6): failure is an offence, with a fine of up to $5,000,000 on indictment.
    - Schedule 6, item 1(a), PDF p.97: "If the computer-system security incident concerned has disrupted, is disrupting or is likely to disrupt the core function ... 12 hours after the CI operator concerned becomes aware of the incident." Item 2: "48 hours after the notification concerned is made under section 28(1)." Item 3: "14 days after the date on which the CI operator concerned becomes aware".
    - Applied: disruption of the core function is confirmed, so the 12-hour limit applies, not 48 hours.
  - **R02**, OCCICS Code of Practice (Generic), v1.0 (a code of practice under Cap. 653 s.8; per s.1.1.4 it "is not subsidiary legislation", but can be admitted in evidence under R01 s.9).
    - s.7.3.3(b), PDF p.35: example "Ransomware attack that causes suspension of an essential service".
    - s.7.3.4, PDF p.35: serious incident "must be notified within 12 hours".
    - s.7.3.5, PDF p.36: awareness test.
    - s.7.3.6(b), PDF p.36: "the CI operator may first make the notification to a designated telephone number ... and then submit a specified form ... within 48 hours".
    - s.7.3.6(c): sector-specific requirements still apply, so Q02a runs alongside this.
- **Missing facts and conditions:**
  - Whether the bank's verified phone number is the Commissioner's "designated telephone number". I treat it as such because the card calls it the verified route for CI incident notification. If it turns out not to be, a notification that states the nature of the incident and names the system still satisfies s.28(2)(b)(ii).
  - Whether a filing route will be available for the 48-hour written record. LC asks on the call; condition owner is Compliance/LC.
  - No internal condition may hold this call (PH01 s.2.4).
- **Internal bank procedure (PH01 v1.0):**
  - s.5.2 names "Cap. 653, section 28 and Schedule 6, and the Commissioner's Code of Practice section 7.3" and "does not restate their triggers, recipients or time limits".
  - s.5.3: a deadline tracker, with each clock "checked by a second LC officer within 30 minutes".
  - s.5.6: standby filing device and alternate route.
  - s.4.1: Severity 1, "a critical operation is disrupted".
  - No conflict with the external requirements.

---

**Governance and clearance**

- No legal or governance condition holds either report.
- LC clears the content. The CMT chair is informed.
- SEC confirms facts in parallel, and its corrections go in the next update.

**Outside the assigned units, for the facilitator's awareness only:**
- Under PH01 s.3, a Police report is LC's decision. I am flagging it for the CMT and not deciding it in this unit.
- PCPD notification is not triggered on current facts, because no data exposure is confirmed. LC will reassess if exposure is found.

LC answer for C02 (Monday 16 Nov 2026, 09:30 HKT, H+1:30). Units: Q05a and Q05b only. I locked this answer before seeing colleagues' answers. The facilitator gave LC no handoff for C02. My C01 answer (Q02a/b) has already been delivered and stands.

**Facts I am using, all from the C02 card:**
- Ransom demand: 6 BTC by 02:00 HKT on Tue 17 Nov.
- The attacker claims to have copied customer files and sent a screenshot of a few rows of identity-like data. Where those rows came from is UNVERIFIED.
- Nobody knows who the attacker is or who controls the wallet. Sanctions and terrorist status are unknown.
- The verified secure filing channel is working again.
- A reporter has asked whether we paid. That question is COM's to answer; LC clears the wording only.

---

## Q05a – Payment posture

**Decision:** Do not pay. The bank's posture is non-payment, and no steps are taken to prepare a payment.
- The 02:00 HKT deadline does not change this. We do not act on the attacker's clock.
- Treasury opens no virtual-asset accounts, buys no BTC and hires no intermediaries.
- LC sends Treasury a written hold today, target 10:30 HKT.
- Only the Board can depart from this posture, and only after the legal gates below are confirmed in writing. LC's recommendation to the Board is that, even then, it should not pay.

**Owners:**
- Board: the payment decision.
- LC: the written legal gates and the recommendation.
- CMT chair: tells the Board chair within 2 hours of the demand. The demand was received by 09:30, so the latest time is 11:30 HKT.
- CFO: notifies the cyber insurer within 24 hours of declaration.
- Treasury: carries out the hold.

**Checks that would constrain or change the posture.** Each must be cleared by LC in writing and then decided by the Board.

1. **Cap. 455 OSCO (statute)**
   - **Rule (R16c, PDF p.82, s.25(1)):** "knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that any property ... represents any person's proceeds of an indictable offence, he deals with that property."
   - **Rule (PDF p.83, s.25A(1)):** anyone who "knows or suspects that any property ... (c) is intended to be used in connection with, an indictable offence" must "as soon as it is reasonable for him to do so disclose that knowledge or suspicion ... to an authorized officer."
   - **Rule (PDF p.83, s.25A(2)(a)):** protection applies only where "that disclosure is made before he does that act and he does that act with the consent of an authorized officer."
   - **Rule (PDF p.6, s.2):** "authorized officer" includes "any police officer". "Dealing" includes "disposing of or converting the property."
   - **How it applies:** A ransom payment would be paid into a channel controlled by the extortioner and would become the proceeds of the extortion. In my professional judgment, that brings s.25A disclosure and consent into play.
   - **Action:** LC reports the extortion and the demanded payment to the Police Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, using the contact route in the Regulator Contact Register (RCR). This is in any case LC's decision under PH01 s.3.
     - Target: by 11:00 HKT today, by phone, followed by a written disclosure.
     - Any payment without prior disclosure and Police consent is barred.
   - **Tipping-off:** s.25A(5) (PDF p.84) makes it an offence to disclose anything "likely to prejudice any investigation". So LC must clear any media or customer wording that refers to the Police report.
   - **Left to judgment:** the exact disclosure route and form. These are not set out in the assigned pages.

2. **Cap. 575 UNATMO (statute)**
   - **Rule (R16d, PDF pp.20-21, s.8(a)):** a person must not "make any property or financial (or related) services available ... to or for the benefit of a person knowing that, or being reckless as to whether, the person is a terrorist or terrorist associate."
   - **Rule (s.8A(1)):** a similar ban on dealing with specified terrorist property.
   - **Rule (PDF p.36, s.12(1)):** disclosure to an authorized officer where a person "knows or suspects" property is terrorist property.
   - **Missing fact:** who the recipient is. With an anonymous wallet, the bank cannot exclude recklessness. Until screening clears the recipient, any payment is barred.

3. **Sanctions screening by external counsel**
   - No direct rule located in assigned sources.
   - Searched all manifest files (PH01, R01–R16d) for "sanction", "virtual asset", "ransom" and "extortion". The only sanctions hit was PH01 s.12.2.
   - Treat this as an internal gate plus professional judgment. Payment is barred until external counsel has screened the recipient.

4. **Police view.** Obtain it under both the OSCO step and PH01. Record it in the RCR.

5. **Insurer position.** CFO to obtain it. This is a contractual check, not a legal permission. It cannot override items 1–3.

6. **Regulators**
   - **HKMA:** Update immediately on the extortion demand and the data claim (PH01 v1.0 s.5.8: "at once on any of: ... an extortion demand"). This is the R05 continuing-update expectation; R05 p.2 says "The HKMA may require the AI concerned to provide further information or updates".
     - Owner: LC. Target: 10:00 HKT. Channel: phone to the supervisory contact, then a written update.
   - **Cap. 653 Commissioner:** Give the same facts as supplementary information through the now-available secure channel. This is also a chance to file the s.28(3) written record early.
   - **Judgment:** the "copied customer files" claim brings PCPD and data-breach assessment into play. That is outside Q05, so I am only flagging it. Data exposure stays "suspected/unverified" until SEC validates the sample (Q04a).

**Professional judgment (rationale):**
- Paying does not guarantee decryption or deletion of the data.
- It would fund crime, and there are unresolved OSCO and UNATMO exposures.
- The bank's recovery is better served by the failover and BCP route.
- The fact that the data claim is unverified does not change the posture. Customer protection is handled through notification and remediation instead.

**Internal bank procedure (PH01 v1.0):**
- s.12.1: "The Board's policy is that the bank does not pay a ransom. Any departure is for the Board alone."
- s.12.2: LC confirms in writing the Cap. 455 position "including any disclosure and consent", Cap. 575 screening, "sanctions screening by external counsel; the Police view; and the insurer's position. Treasury holds all preparatory steps ... until the Board decides."
- s.15.1: tell the Board chair within two hours of "an extortion demand".
- s.11.3 (for COM's reply, cleared by LC): "never denies receipt of a demand. It states whether a payment has been made only as a verified present fact."
- No conflict with external law. The internal gates are stricter than the statutes and consistent with them.

---

## Q05b – Contact with the attacker

**Decision:** No contact authorised at this point. No reply, no request for proof or further samples, no negotiation and no request for an extension.

**Condition for any future contact:** Only if LC and SEC jointly recommend it in writing, for a stated limited purpose (for example, if the Police ask for it). The CMT chair must authorise it in writing after consulting the Police.

**Who may act:**
- Authorises: CMT chair, in writing.
- Recommends: LC and SEC jointly.
- Conducts: one designated specialist on a segregated channel, keeping a full transcript that SEC enters into evidence.
- Nobody else replies. Branches, the contact centre, COM and vendors pass any attacker message to SEC.

**Timing:** Effective now (09:30 HKT).
- LC and SEC review the position after the Police consultation, target 11:00 HKT. They then tell the CMT whether any limited-purpose contact should be recommended.
- Default if there is no recommendation: no contact.

**How the instruction goes out:** CMT decision log, then a staff instruction through COM's frontline scripts (Q06a). COM approves; LC clears.

**Basis:**
- **Direct external rule:** none located in the assigned sources.
  - Searched all manifest files for "attacker", "extortion", "ransom" and "contact with". Only PH01 hits governed contact.
- **Relevant external principles:**
  - R05 p.2 (supervisory circular): public communications should weigh "whether a public announcement may prejudice any ongoing criminal proceedings or any investigation."
  - OSCO s.25A(5) on tipping-off.
- **Professional judgment:**
  - Contact risks prejudicing the Police investigation.
  - It signals willingness to pay and invites more demands.
  - It can expose more data, because samples are only received into the evidence process.
- **Internal bank procedure (PH01 v1.0):**
  - s.12.3: "None, unless the CMT chair authorises it in writing on a joint LC and SEC recommendation, for a stated limited purpose, after consulting the Police. Contact is made only by one designated specialist on a segregated channel, with a full transcript."
  - s.6.6: "Nobody requests further samples, visits attacker links or uploads attacker material to an outside service."
  - No conflict with external sources.

---

## Simulated actions for the facilitator to log

| Time (HKT) | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 09:35 | Non-payment posture and no-contact decision entered in the CMT decision log | LC |
| By 10:00 | HKMA phone update on the extortion and data claim; written update to follow | LC |
| By 10:00 | LC clears COM's reply to the reporter. Must not deny receipt of a demand. Must say no payment has been made only if that is verified as a present fact. Must not mention the Police report in any way that could prejudice the investigation | LC |
| By 10:30 | Written Treasury hold | LC |
| By 11:00 | Police CSTCB report and Cap. 455 s.25A disclosure | LC |
| By 11:30 | Board chair informed | CMT chair |
| Asap | Commissioner given supplementary information through the secure channel | LC |
| Within 24h of declaration | Insurer notified | CFO |

Receipts for each item are logged under PH01 s.5.5.

**Decision:** Do not pay. The bank's posture is non-payment, and no steps are taken to prepare a payment.

- Treasury opens no virtual-asset accounts, buys no BTC and hires no intermediaries.
- LC sends Treasury a written hold today, target 10:30 HKT.
- Only the Board can depart from this posture, and only after the legal gates below are confirmed in writing. LC's recommendation to the Board is that, even then, it should not pay.

**Owners:**
- Board: the payment decision.
- LC: the written legal gates and the recommendation.
- CMT chair: tells the Board chair within 2 hours of the demand. The demand was received by 09:30, so the latest time is 11:30 HKT.
- CFO: notifies the cyber insurer within 24 hours of declaration.
- Treasury: carries out the hold.

**Checks that would constrain or change the posture.** Each must be cleared by LC in writing and then decided by the Board.

1. **Cap. 455 OSCO (statute)**
   - **Rule (R16c, PDF p.82, s.25(1)):** "knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that any property ... represents any person's proceeds of an indictable offence, he deals with that property."
   - **Rule (PDF p.83, s.25A(1)):** anyone who "knows or suspects that any property ... (c) is intended to be used in connection with, an indictable offence" must "as soon as it is reasonable for him to do so disclose that knowledge or suspicion ... to an authorized officer."
   - **Rule (PDF p.83, s.25A(2)(a)):** protection applies only where "that disclosure is made before he does that act and he does that act with the consent of an authorized officer."
   - **Rule (PDF p.6, s.2):** "authorized officer" includes "any police officer". "Dealing" includes "disposing of or converting the property."
   - **How it applies:** A ransom payment would be paid into a channel controlled by the extortioner and would become the proceeds of the extortion. In my professional judgment, that brings s.25A disclosure and consent into play.
   - **Action:** LC reports the extortion and the demanded payment to the Police Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, using the contact route in the Regulator Contact Register (RCR). This is in any case LC's decision under PH01 s.3.
     - Target: by 11:00 HKT today, by phone, followed by a written disclosure.
     - Any payment without prior disclosure and Police consent is barred.
   - **Tipping-off:** s.25A(5) (PDF p.84) makes it an offence to disclose anything "likely to prejudice any investigation". So LC must clear any media or customer wording that refers to the Police report.
   - **Left to judgment:** the exact disclosure route and form. These are not set out in the assigned pages.

2. **Cap. 575 UNATMO (statute)**
   - **Rule (R16d, PDF pp.20-21, s.8(a)):** a person must not "make any property or financial (or related) services available ... to or for the benefit of a person knowing that, or being reckless as to whether, the person is a terrorist or terrorist associate."
   - **Rule (s.8A(1)):** a similar ban on dealing with specified terrorist property.
   - **Rule (PDF p.36, s.12(1)):** disclosure to an authorized officer where a person "knows or suspects" property is terrorist property.
   - **Missing fact:** who the recipient is. With an anonymous wallet, the bank cannot exclude recklessness. Until screening clears the recipient, any payment is barred.

3. **Sanctions screening by external counsel**
   - No direct rule located in assigned sources.
   - Searched all manifest files (PH01, R01–R16d) for "sanction", "virtual asset", "ransom" and "extortion". The only sanctions hit was PH01 s.12.2.

=== PDF page 1 ===
Guidance Note
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and
Data Breach Notifications
INTRODUCTION
Good data breach handling makes good business
sense
A good data breach handling policy and practice is
not only useful for containing the damage caused
by a breach, but also demonstrate the data user’s
responsibility and accountability when tackling the
problem, by formulating a clear action plan that
can be followed in the event of a data breach. In
addition to enabling the data subjects affected by
the breach to take appropriate protective measures,
data breach notifications can help reduce the risk of
litigation and maintain the data user’s goodwill and
business relationships, and in some cases the public’s
confidence in the organisation.
This guidance is aimed at assisting data users to
prepare for and handle data breaches, to prevent
recurrence and to mitigate the loss and damage
caused to the data subjects involved, particularly
when sensitive personal data is involved.
What is personal data?
Data breach incidents often involve the personal
data of individuals, such as customers, service users,
employees and job applicants of organisations.
Under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance
(Chapter 486 of the Laws of Hong Kong) (PDPO),
personal data means any data1
(a) relating directly or indirectly to a living
individual;
(b) from which it is practicable for the identity
of the individual to be directly or indirectly
ascertained; and
(c) in a form in which access to or processing of the
data is practicable.
What is a data breach?
A data breach is generally regarded as a suspected
or actual breach of the security of personal data
held by a data user2, which exposes the personal
data of data subject(s) to the risk of unauthorised or
accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use.
The following are some examples of data
breaches:
ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ The loss of personal data stored on devices
such as laptop computers, USB flash drives,
portable hard disks or backup tapes
The improper handling of personal data,
such as improper disposal, sending emails
to unintended parties or the unauthorised
access of databases by employees
A database containing personal data that
is hacked or accessed by outsiders without
authorisation
The disclosure of personal data to a third
party who obtained the data by deception
The leakage of data caused by the installation
of file-sharing software on a computer
1 Section 2(1) of the PDPO.
2 Under section 2(1) of the PDPO, a "data user", in relation to personal data, means a person who, either alone or jointly or in common with
other persons, controls the collection, holding, processing or use of the data.
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 1
June 2023

=== PDF page 2 ===
A data breach may amount to a contravention of
Data Protection Principle (DPP) 4(1) and (2) in
Schedule 1 to the PDPO. DPP 4(1) provides that
a data user shall take all reasonably practicable
steps to ensure that the personal data it holds is
protected against unauthorised or accidental access,
processing, erasure, loss or use, having particular
regard to:
(a) the kind of data and the harm that could result
if any of those things should occur;
(b) the physical location where the data is stored;
(c) any security measures incorporated (whether
by automated means or otherwise) into any
equipment in which the data is stored;
(d) any measures taken for ensuring the integrity,
prudence and competence of persons having
access to the data; and
(e) any measures taken for ensuring the secure
transmission of the data.
DPP 4(2) provides that if a data user engages a
data processor,3 whether within or outside Hong
Kong, to process personal data on the data user’s
behalf, the data user must adopt contractual or
other means, to prevent unauthorised or accidental
access, processing, erasure, loss or use of the data
transferred to the data processor for processing.
What are the common causes of data breaches in
Hong Kong?
Data breaches may result from a variety of causes.
Some common causes include:
•
Cyberattacks
Given the value of personal data, organisations
may fall prey to cyberattacks (e.g., ransomware,
brute force attacks, distributed denial-of-
service attacks or phishing), which may result
in unauthorised access to, or even exfiltration
of, the personal data stored in their servers or
databases.
•
•
•
•
•
System misconfigurations
System configuration and administration errors
can cause data breaches. Examples include
unauthorised access to personal data where data
systems allow access without authentications or
access-rights controls.
Loss of physical documents or portable devices
Data breaches often result from the loss of
physical documents or portable devices
containing personal data, such as letters,
completed forms, USB storage devices or laptop
computers. Data processors contracted to handle
personal data on a data user’s behalf may also
inadvertently cause data loss.
Improper/wrongful disposal of personal data
Documents in various formats that contain
personal data (e.g., hard disks, paper files, USB
drives or other types of data storage devices)
may be accidentally or improperly disposed
of without adhering to organisational policies
concerning document destruction, and thus the
data contained in such documents may be at risk.
Inadvertent disclosure by email or by post
Digital files or physical documents containing
personal data can be inadvertently sent
to unintended recipients, resulting in the
unauthorised disclosure of attachments that may
contain personal data.
Staff negligence/misconduct
This mainly refers to situations where staff of an
organisation who have been granted valid access
rights mishandle personal data either purposely,
accidentally and/or maliciously.
3 According to DPP 2(4) and DPP4(3), "data processor" means a person who processes personal data on behalf of another person and does not
process the data for any of the person’s own purposes.
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 2
June 2023

=== PDF page 3 ===
PREPARING FOR CONTINGENCY – DATA BREACH RESPONSE PLAN
A data breach response plan is a document setting
out how an organisation will respond in the event
of a data breach. A comprehensive data breach
response plan helps ensure a quick response to and
effective management of a data breach. The plan
should outline a set of procedures to be followed
in the event of a data breach and the data user’s
strategy for identifying, containing, assessing and
managing the impact brought about by the incident
from start to finish. A prompt response to a data
breach may substantially minimise and contain the
impact of a breach.
The plan is recommended to cover the
following aspects (non-exhaustive):
ØØ A description of what constitutes a data
breach with examples tailored to the
nature of the organisation, and the criteria
that trigger the implementation of the data
breach response plan
ØØ An internal incident notification
procedure to escalate the breach to the
senior management, the data protection
officer and/or dedicated data breach
response team, incorporating a standard
form to facilitate the reporting of the
required information
ØØ The designation of the roles and
responsibilities of members of the
dedicated breach response team (e.g., the
data protection officer may assume overall
responsibility for handling a data breach
incident; the information technology
department for identifying the location of
potentially compromised data and taking
remedial measures; and the customer
service department for addressing the
issues of affected individuals and for
providing updates to customers)
ØØ ØØ A contact list with contact details of all
breach response team members (e.g., the
core management, chief data protection
officer, information technology experts,
risk management and human resources
professionals)
A risk assessment workflow to assess the
likelihood and severity of the harm caused
to the affected data subjects as a result of
the breach
ØØ A containment strategy for containing
and remedying the breach
ØØ A communication plan covering the
criteria and threshold for determining
whether the affected data subjects,
regulatory authorities and other
relevant parties should be notified;
the kind of information that must be
provided; the point of contact in the
organisation responsible for liaising with
the stakeholders; and the methods of
notification
ØØ An investigation procedure f o r
investigating the breach and reporting the
results to the senior management
ØØ A record-keeping policy to ensure that
the incident is properly documented as
the relevant records may be required by
regulatory authorities or law enforcement
agencies
ØØ A post-incident review mechanism for
identifying areas that require improvement
to prevent future recurrence
ØØ A training or drill plan to ensure that all
relevant staff can follow the procedures
properly when dealing with a data breach
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 3
June 2023

=== PDF page 4 ===
HANDLING DATA BREACHES
The proper handling and management of a data
breach demonstrates the data user’s commitment to
tackling the problem and may substantially reduce
the impact of a breach on affected individuals
and the potential reputational damage to the
organisation. The following steps are recommended
when handling a data breach.
Step 1: Immediate gathering of essential information
As a starting point, the data user shall promptly
gather all relevant information of the data
breach to assess the impact on data subjects and
to identify appropriate mitigation measures.
Questions such as the following should be
addressed:
•
When did the breach occur?
•
Where did the breach occur?
•
How was the breach detected and by whom?
•
What was the cause of the breach?
•
What kind of personal data was involved?
•
How many data subjects might be affected?
•
What harm may have been caused to those
affected individuals?
The staff members who first discover the breach
should consider whether to escalate the incident
to the dedicated data breach response team/senior
management/data protection officer, according
to the procedures laid down in the data breach
response plan.
Step 2: Containing the data breach
After detecting the breach and conducting
an initial assessment, the data user should
immediately take steps to contain the breach as
effectively as possible. Remedial actions to lessen
the harm or damage that may be caused to the
affected data subjects should be taken.
Depending on the categories of personal
data involved and the severity of the breach,
the following containment measures (non-
exhaustive) may be considered:
ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ Conducting a thorough search for the lost
items containing personal data
Requesting the unintended recipients of
emails/letters/fax to delete or return the
mistakenly sent documents
Requesting internet companies to remove
any relevant cached links from their search
engines
Shutting down or isolating the compromised/
breached system/server and thoroughly
checking whether other interconnected
systems containing personal data are
affected
ØØ Disabling system functions that may be
relevant to the breach
ØØ Fixing any bugs or errors that may have
caused the breach
ØØ ØØ Alerting banks or credit card companies,
which may help reduce the risk of financial
losses for the affected data subjects
Keeping records of the occurrence of the
breach and all follow-up actions taken to
facilitate investigations and for the taking
of corrective actions
ØØ Notifying the relevant law enforcement
agencies if identity theft or other criminal
activities have been or are likely to be
committed
ØØ Requiring the data processor to take
immediate remedial measures and to
notify the data user of the progress in the
event that the data breach is caused by an
act or omission by the data processor
ØØ Remotely wiping a lost or stolen electronic
device
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 4
June 2023

=== PDF page 5 ===
ØØ Changing users' passwords and system
configurations to block any (further)
unauthorised access
ØØ Removing the access rights of users
suspected to have committed or
contributed to the data breach
ØØ Keeping a proper record of the compromised
system for further investigation
ØØ Considering whether technical assistance
is required
Step 3: Assessing the risk of harm
Once all essential information has been gathered,
the data users should then ensure that they
understand the risks of harm that may be caused to
the affected individuals, so that they can take steps
to limit the impact. The possible harm caused by a
data breach may include:
•
Threats to personal safety
•
Identity theft
•
Financial loss
•
Humiliation or loss of dignity, damage to
reputation or relationships
•
Loss of business or employment opportunities
The extent of the harm suffered by the
affected data subjects in a data breach
depends on:
ØØ The kind and sensitivity of the personal
data being leaked: generally, the more
sensitive the data, the higher the risk of
harm that may be caused to the affected
data subjects
ØØ The amount of personal data involved:
in general, the greater the volume of
personal data leaked, the more serious the
consequences will be
ØØ The circumstances of the data breach:
online data leakage is difficult to be
effectively contained and the further
dissemination and use of the leaked data
is thus a risk. However, if the recipients of
the data are known and traceable, the data
breach may be easier to contain
ØØ The nature of harm
ØØ The likelihood of identity theft or fraud:
sometimes, the leaked data, either
independently in itself or when combined
with other data, can facilitate the
commission of identity theft or fraud. For
example, a combination of Hong Kong
Identity Card information, date of birth,
address, credit card details and bank
account information is more likely to result
in identity theft
ØØ Whether a backup of the lost data is
available
ØØ Whether the leaked data are adequately
encrypted, anonymised or otherwise
rendered inaccessible, e.g., if access is
password-protected
ØØ ØØ The duration of the breach
Whether the breach is an isolated incident
or a systematic problem
ØØ In the case of physical loss, whether the
lost items have been found before they
could be accessed or copied
ØØ Whether effective mitigation/remedial
measures have been taken after the breach
has occurred
ØØ The ability of the data subjects to avoid or
mitigate possible harm
ØØ The affected data subjects’ reasonable
expectations of personal data privacy
Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications 5
June 2023

=== PDF page 6 ===
The result of an assessment may reveal a real risk
of harm, for example, when a database containing
personal particulars, contact details and financial
data is accidentally leaked online through file-
sharing software, many breaches may entail. On the
other hand, a lower risk of harm may be involved in,
for example, the loss of a USB flash drive containing
securely encrypted data which may not be sensitive
in nature, or when the lost or misplaced device
containing personal data has subsequently been
found and the personal data does not appear to
have been accessed.
Step 4: Considering giving data breach
notifications
When deciding whether to report a breach to the
affected data subjects, the PCPD and other law
enforcement agencies, the data user should take into
account the potential consequences of a breach for
the affected individuals, how serious or substantial
these are, and how likely they are to happen. The
consequences of failing to give notification should
also be duly considered.
In general, the data user should notify the
PCPD and the affected data subjects as soon as
practicable after becoming aware of the data
breach, particularly if the data breach is likely to
result in a real risk of harm to those affected data
subjects. Data users subject to other regulatory
requirements may also need to report data breaches
in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions,
codes of practice, rules or guidelines.4 Notification
obligations under the laws and regulations of other
jurisdictions5 may also be triggered. If necessary, the
data user should seek professional advice regarding
compliance with such requirements.
Step 5: Documenting the breach
A data user should learn from the data breach
incident, facilitate a post-breach review and improve
personal data handling practices as appropriate. A
comprehensive record of the incident is therefore
required, which should include all facts relating to
the breach, ranging from details of the breach and
its effects to the containment and remedial actions
taken by the data user. Organisations that are
required to comply with the laws and regulations
of other jurisdictions should also consider
whether there are any mandatory documentation
requirements under those laws and regulations6
.

DATA BREACH NOTIFICATIONS
A data breach notification is a formal notification
given by the data user to the relevant parties
including the affected data subjects and the
PCPD. This can help to:
•
Draw the affected data subjects’ attention to
take proactive steps or measures to mitigate
any potential harm or damage, for example,
to protect their physical safety, reputation or
financial position;
•
Enable the relevant authorities to undertake
appropriate investigative or follow-up actions;
•
Demonstrate the data user’s commitment to
robust personal data privacy management by
adhering to the principles of transparency and
accountability;
•
Raise public awareness, for example in situations
if public health or security is affected by the data
breach; and
•
Obtain appropriate advice from the PCPD in
terms of promptly responding to the breach
and improving personal data systems and
policies, thus preventing the recurrence of similar
incidents.
To whom should the notification be given?
The data user should consider the circumstances of
the case and decide whether any of the following
parties should be notified as soon as practicable:
•
The affected data subjects
•
The PCPD
•
Law enforcement agencies other than the PCPD
•
Any relevant regulators
•
Other parties who may be able to take remedial
actions, such as protecting the personal data
privacy and the interests of the data subjects
affected (for example, Internet companies like
Google and Yahoo may assist to remove relevant
cached links from their search engines)
What should be included in the notification?
Depending on the circumstances of the case, a
data breach notification may include:
ØØ ØØ ØØ A general description of what occurred
The date and time of the breach and its
duration (or an estimate)
The date and time when the breach was
detected
ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ ØØ The source of the breach (either the data
user or the third party that processed the
personal data on its behalf)
Basic information about the type of breach
A list of the types of personal data involved
The categories and approximate number
of data subjects involved
The categories and approximate number
of personal data records involved
An assessment of the risk of harm (such
as identity theft or fraud) that could result
from the breach
ØØ A description of the measures taken or to
be taken to mitigate the loss or to prevent
further unauthorised access to and/or
leakage of personal data
ØØ The contact information of the data
breach response team or of a staff member
designated to handle the data breach
ØØ Information and advice on the actions
the data subjects can take to protect
themselves from any adverse effects of
the breach and from identity theft or fraud
(e.g., resetting passwords, being alert to
phishing emails or fraudulent activity
on their accounts, contacting financial
institutions to change their credit card
details, requesting that credit reference
agencies suspend any provision of their
credit reports to third parties)

Data users should consider the circumstances of
the case and seek legal advice if they are uncertain
about the content of the information to be included
in the notification.
When to notify?
A notification must be given in sufficient time for its
benefits to be maximised, in particular to reduce the
risk of harm caused to the affected data subjects and
to maintain the data user’s goodwill. A notification
should generally be given as soon as practicable
after becoming aware of the incident, regardless
of the progress of any internal investigation. If
the data user is initially unable to provide full details
about the breach, providing as much information
as possible in the notification is still desirable.
After the full details of the incident are revealed, all
information should be submitted to the PCPD and
other law enforcement agencies without delay.
As there may be specified notification time frames
in other jurisdictions, if notification to overseas
regulatory authorities is required, the data user
should seek professional advice, if necessary, and
ensure that the notification is made within the
statutory time limit in accordance with the relevant
requirements.
How to notify?
•
Notification to the data subjects
The data subjects can be notified directly by phone,
in writing, via email or in person.
When a direct data breach notification is not
practicable in the circumstan ces, for example, if
data subjects are not immediately identifiable or if
public interest exists, then public announcements,
newspaper advertisements or announcements on
websites or social media platforms may be more
effective. If a data breach results in particularly
serious harm or affects a large number of individuals,
using multiple methods to publicise the breach is a
reasonable approach.

In July 2008, the HKMA issued a circular “Customer Data Protection” reminding authorized
institutions (AIs) of the importance of protecting the confidentiality of customer data and

the industry and technologies over the past several years, I am writing to update certain

Controls for preventing and detecting loss or leakage of customer data
To protect the confidentiality of customer data, AIs should ensure a high degree of alertness
among staff members in protecting customer data. Moreover, AIs should implement “layers”
of security controls (covering both IT and non-IT controls) to prevent and detect any loss or
leakage of customer data. Although various Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) modules1
and circulars have already covered risk management principles and control measures that are
useful for protecting customer data, we have elaborated and updated certain control measures
as set out in the Annex of this circular. We have taken into account the latest developments,
particularly:

automatic tools) in the banking industry for preventing or detecting the leakage of
customer data. Accordingly, the relevant AIs are better prepared to prevent and detect
incidents involving leakage of customer data and take prompt actions to contain the
impact so as to reduce their reputation and legal risks. For example, these AIs could
more promptly identify cases caused by individual staff members (e.g. who transmit
customer data to personal email accounts without permission) so as to take timely
actions to avoid further leakage of customer data;
